definition: Digital fashion is a field of fashion design that relies on 3D software or artificial intelligence to produce hyper-realistic, data-intensive digital 3D garment simulations that are digital-only products or digital models for physical products.
details: Digital garments can be worn and presented in virtual environments, social media, online gaming, virtual reality (VR), and augmented reality (AR) platforms. The field aims to contribute to the development of a more sustainable future for the fashion industry. It has been praised as a possible answer to ethical and creative concerns of traditional fashion by promoting innovation, reducing waste, and encouraging conscious consumption. However, empirical research has questioned whether digital fashion communities embody the radical and anti-consumerist values they claim. A 2025 study presented by YeSeung Lee at the FACTUM international conference on fashion communication analysed 88,141 posts across nine platforms over eight months using Pulsar. It found that only 4.8% of author biographies indicated any sociopolitical focus, and that discourse predominantly relied on generic slogans and trending buzzwords, primarily reinforcing existing fashion hierarchies and consumerist frameworks rather than challenging them. explainer.lead: Digital fashion uses 3D software or artificial intelligence to create garments that exist online, serve as models for physical clothing, or both. It could reduce waste and support new forms of creative expression, although its sustainability and anti-consumerist claims should not be taken for granted.

tiers.eli5: It is like designing clothes for a video-game character instead of cutting cloth for a person. The outfit can look very real and appear in games, virtual worlds, or social media, and a digital version can also help plan clothing that will later be made from fabric.
tiers.practitioner: Practitioners use 3D software, and sometimes AI, to produce hyper-realistic, data-intensive garment simulations for virtual presentation or as digital models of physical products. Outputs may be prepared for social media, online games, VR, or AR. A convincing simulation does not itself demonstrate reduced waste or changed consumption, so those claims need separate evaluation.
tiers.paperLevel: Digital fashion is a field of fashion design that uses 3D software or AI to produce hyper-realistic, data-intensive 3D garment simulations, either as digital-only products or as digital models for physical products. Its proposed benefits include innovation, waste reduction, and conscious consumption, but these remain contested. A 2025 study presented by YeSeung Lee analysed 88,141 posts across nine platforms over eight months using Pulsar; only 4.8% of author biographies indicated a sociopolitical focus, and the discourse largely reinforced existing fashion hierarchies and consumerist frameworks.

explainer.example: A designer creates a hyper-realistic 3D jacket, displays it on an avatar in an online game, and uses the same digital garment as the model for a jacket that may later be manufactured physically.

explainer.intuition: Treat clothing as a detailed 3D digital object rather than starting only with fabric. The same garment can then be displayed on virtual bodies or used to represent a future physical product.
howItWorks: Create a garment design for digital-only use or for a physical product.
Use 3D software or AI to build a hyper-realistic, data-intensive garment simulation.
Present the garment on virtual bodies or in digital environments.
Deploy it through social media, online gaming, VR, or AR, or retain it as a model for physical production.
explainer.whyItMatters: Digital fashion expands where clothing can be designed, worn, and presented, while offering a possible route to less waste and more conscious consumption. Research into its communities also shows that digital presentation alone does not guarantee radical, anti-consumerist, or socially engaged practice.
misconceptions: Digital fashion is not limited to virtual-only clothing; it also includes digital models for physical products.
A digital garment is not automatically sustainable or anti-consumerist merely because it uses less physical material in its presentation.
